definition: Direct voice input (DVI), sometimes called voice input control (VIC), is a style of human–machine interaction "HMI" in which the user makes voice commands to issue instructions to the machine through speech recognition.
details: In the field of military aviation, DVI has been introduced into the cockpits of several modern military aircraft, such as the Eurofighter Typhoon, the Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II, the Dassault Rafale, the KF-21 Boramae and the Saab JAS 39 Gripen. Such systems have also been used for various other purposes, including industry control systems and speech recognition assistance for impaired individuals.

explainer.lead: Direct voice input lets a person control a machine by speaking commands instead of entering instructions through another interface. It is used in modern military aircraft, industrial control systems, and assistance for impaired individuals.

tiers.eli5: It is like telling a helpful robot what to do with your voice. You speak a command, the machine works out the words, and then it follows the instruction. This can help a pilot control aircraft systems or help someone who finds other controls difficult to use.
tiers.practitioner: Implementations use speech recognition to turn a spoken command into an instruction for a cockpit, industrial controller, or assistive interface. Engineering work centres on the command set, the mapping from recognized speech to actions, and checks for recognition errors, especially where an incorrect action matters.
tiers.paperLevel: DVI is a human–machine interaction style in which spoken commands are converted by speech recognition into machine instructions; it is also called voice input control (VIC). It describes the command-input method rather than a particular recognition algorithm, and recognition errors can affect whether an instruction is carried out correctly.

explainer.example: A pilot speaks a cockpit command. The DVI system recognizes the command and issues the corresponding instruction to the aircraft system, without requiring the pilot to type it.

explainer.intuition: The basic idea is to make speech a control channel: say what the machine should do, and let speech recognition turn that command into an instruction.
howItWorks: A speech-recognition system interprets the speech.
The recognized command is mapped to a machine instruction.
The machine carries out the requested action.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides a direct way to instruct machines through speech in demanding cockpit settings, industrial control, and assistive interfaces.
misconceptions: DVI is not limited to military aircraft; it also appears in industrial and assistive systems.
It is not a specific speech-recognition algorithm, but a style of human–machine interaction.
Recognizing speech does not guarantee that every command will be interpreted correctly.
